# A map of the viruses

> *Virologists sort viruses by genome and structure, but a patient catches a virus by a route: a
> breath, a meal, a needle or a mosquito bite. Structure predicts how a virus survives, changes and
> can be treated, and the route predicts who catches it and how its spread is prevented.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Describe a virus by its genome, envelope, main route of spread and persistence.
- Distinguish a virus group named for a family from one named for a route of spread, and give an
  example of each.
- Predict from its envelope how well a virus survives outside the body and by which routes it can
  spread.
- Relate the genome of a virus on the map to how fast it changes, and to what follows for vaccines
  and drugs.
- Relate persistence to spread without symptoms, to disease years after infection and to screening.
- Name the group a virus belongs to from a few of its traits.
:::

## How viruses are grouped {#sec-vmap-grouping}

Four traits describe a virus well enough to place it: its genome, whether it has an envelope, the
route by which it spreads, and whether it persists after the first illness. The first two are fixed
by the structure of the virion (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-structure)); the last two describe how the
virus reaches its host and whether it stays. A virus that does not stay causes an **acute
infection**: rapid onset, then either clearance or death of the host. A virus that stays causes a
**latent infection**, persistence of an organism in a silent state, with the possibility of
reactivation, or a **chronic infection**, infection and inflammation continuing for months or years
(see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)).

::: {.example}
Influenza virus is an enveloped virus with a negative-sense RNA genome that spreads in respiratory
particles and causes acute infection.
:::

Viruses are grouped either by genome and structure or by route of spread, and the two groupings
predict different things.

### By genome and structure {#sec-vmap-structure}

Virologists classify viruses into families, each a set of related viruses that share a kind of
genome, a way of copying it and a structure. Genome and structure predict three things about a
virus:

- How well it survives outside the body, which depends on whether it has an envelope
- Which enzymes it must bring or encode to copy its genome, and so which drugs can act on it
- How fast it changes, which depends on whether the enzyme that copies its genome proofreads (checks
  each base as it is added and removes a wrong one)

The viruses on the map have five kinds of genome, and the kind of genome decides which enzymes the
virus must carry or encode (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)).

| Genome | Viruses on the map |
|---|---|
| DNA | Herpesviruses, adenoviruses, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B virus |
| Positive-sense RNA | SARS-CoV-2, rhinoviruses, norovirus, enteroviruses, hepatitis A, C and E viruses, dengue virus, Zika virus, chikungunya virus, Japanese encephalitis virus |
| Negative-sense RNA | Influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, measles virus |
| Double-stranded RNA | Rotavirus |
| Retrovirus: RNA copied into DNA | HIV |

### By route of spread {#sec-vmap-route}

Grouped by route of spread (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)), viruses from unrelated
families fall together, and the route predicts who is exposed and which measures interrupt spread.
Spread by bites needs a **vector**, an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts.

| Route | What carries the virus | Who is exposed | Main means of prevention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Respiratory | Particles breathed out, and hands that carry secretions to the nose and eyes | People who share air or are in close contact with an infected person | Vaccines against several; ventilation, masks and hand hygiene |
| Faecal–oral | Water, food, hands and surfaces contaminated with faeces | People without safe water or food, and people living in close quarters, such as care homes | Safe water, sanitation, food hygiene and hand washing; vaccines against some |
| Blood and sexual contact | Blood, semen and vaginal fluid, and passage from mother to child | Sexual partners, people exposed to blood or shared needles, and infants of infected mothers | Screening of donated blood and of pregnant women; sterile needles and condoms; antiviral drugs that make an infected person less infectious or that protect before exposure; vaccines against some |
| Arthropod bite | A mosquito or tick that has fed on an infected host | People where the vector lives and bites | Removing breeding sites and preventing bites; vaccines against some |

### Where group names come from {#sec-vmap-names}

Virus group names come from three sources.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sources of virus group names]{.tree-title}

- A family: related viruses that share a genome and a structure
  - Herpesviruses: enveloped, with double-stranded DNA, latent for life
- A route of spread
  - Respiratory viruses, viruses spread by the faecal–oral route, and blood-borne and sexually
    transmitted viruses
  - Arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses)
- The organ infected
  - Hepatitis viruses A, B, C and E: unrelated viruses that all infect the liver
:::

An **arbovirus** (arthropod-borne virus) is a virus carried between vertebrate hosts by blood-feeding
arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, in which it multiplies. The name says how the virus travels
and nothing about its structure, so a group named for a route can cut across families.

::: {.example}
Dengue, Zika and Japanese encephalitis viruses belong to one family and are carried by mosquitoes,
while hepatitis C virus belongs to the same family and spreads in blood. Chikungunya virus, carried
by the same mosquitoes as dengue virus, belongs to a different family.
:::

A name taken from the organ says least about the virus. Hepatitis A and E viruses spread by the
faecal–oral route and cause acute infection, whereas hepatitis B and C viruses spread in blood and
can persist for decades. The four belong to four different families and to two different groups.

The five groups of the viral world take their names from one family and four routes:

| Group | Named for | What most members share | Members on the map (main; supporting) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [*Respiratory viruses*](respiratory-viruses.qmd) | Route: respiratory particles and hands | Enveloped RNA viruses that infect the airway; acute infection, often repeated | Influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus; rhinoviruses, adenoviruses, measles virus |
| [*Viruses spread by the faecal–oral route*](enteric-viruses.qmd) | Route: from faeces to mouth | Non-enveloped RNA viruses that survive drying, acid and bile; infect the gut or reach the liver from it; acute infection | Norovirus, rotavirus, enteroviruses; hepatitis A and E viruses |
| [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd) | Route: blood, sexual contact, mother to child | DNA and RNA viruses, several of which persist for years without symptoms | HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus; human papillomavirus |
| [*Arthropod-borne viruses*](arboviruses.qmd) | Route: the bite of a mosquito or tick | Enveloped RNA viruses whose spread follows the vector; acute infection | Dengue virus, Zika virus, chikungunya virus; Japanese encephalitis virus |
| [*Herpesviruses*](herpesviruses.qmd) | Family | Enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses, latent for life after the first infection | Herpes simplex viruses, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus; Epstein–Barr virus |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is "stomach flu" caused by influenza virus?
Vomiting and diarrhoea that spread through a household or a ward are often called "stomach flu", and
the name suggests that influenza virus causes them and that the influenza vaccine prevents them. The
belief comes from the loose use of "flu" for any short illness with fever and aching. Viral
gastroenteritis, the illness the name usually refers to, is caused mostly by norovirus and, in young
children, rotavirus. Both are non-enveloped viruses of the faecal–oral group, unrelated to influenza
virus, which is an enveloped respiratory virus, and the influenza vaccine does not protect against
them.
:::

## What the traits predict {#sec-vmap-predict}

### The envelope predicts survival and route {#sec-vmap-envelope}

Drying, detergents, alcohol and bile disrupt a lipid envelope, whereas a capsid alone withstands them
much better (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-envelope)). On the map, the envelope lines up
with the route of spread:

- Every faecal–oral virus on the map is non-enveloped. Each must survive on hands, in food or water,
  and through stomach acid and bile before it reaches the cells it infects.
- The enveloped viruses travel in ways that spare them from drying: in respiratory particles (mostly
  between people who are close together), in blood and genital fluids, inside a mosquito, or by
  direct contact with saliva or skin. Measles and varicella-zoster viruses are carried farther,
  through the air across a room.
- Rhinoviruses and adenoviruses, the respiratory viruses without an envelope, also spread on hands
  and surfaces.

::: {.example}
Hepatitis A virus and hepatitis B virus both infect the liver. Hepatitis A virus has no envelope and
survives in water and food contaminated with faeces; hepatitis B virus is enveloped and passes in
blood and sexual fluids.
:::

The envelope predicts survival only roughly. Hepatitis B virus, although enveloped, stays infectious
in dried blood on surfaces for at least a week, so it can spread on a shared razor or toothbrush or
on unsterile medical or dental equipment (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted
viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hbv)).

The envelope also predicts the choice of hand hygiene. Alcohol hand rub inactivates enveloped viruses
readily, whereas soap and water, which remove viruses physically, are more reliable against the
non-enveloped viruses of the faecal–oral group (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-resistance)).

### The genome predicts how fast a virus changes {#sec-vmap-change}

Most RNA viruses copy their genomes with polymerases that do not proofread, and retroviruses copy
theirs with a reverse transcriptase that does not proofread either, so both accumulate mutations
faster than DNA viruses (see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-mutation)). Most of
the viruses on the map are RNA viruses, and they include the viruses whose change has the clearest
consequences for vaccines and drugs (see [*How viruses
change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-consequences)):

- Influenza virus, whose vaccine is updated as the virus drifts
- Norovirus, whose new variants infect people who have been infected before
- HIV, which becomes resistant to any single drug and is therefore treated with a combination of
  drugs

Herpesviruses, adenoviruses and human papillomavirus copy their DNA with polymerases that proofread,
so they change slowly. Hepatitis B virus, although a DNA virus, copies its genome by way of an RNA
copy, using its own reverse transcriptase, which does not proofread, so it changes faster than the
other DNA viruses on the map (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted
viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hbv)).

### Persistence predicts silent spread and late disease {#sec-vmap-persistence}

Most viruses on the map cause acute infection: they multiply, are shed for days to weeks and are
cleared. The others persist after the first illness, as latent or chronic infection (see [*Viruses
and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-persistence)).

| Persistence | Viruses on the map | What follows |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | The respiratory, faecal–oral and arthropod-borne viruses, in people with normal immunity | Spread during a short illness; protection afterwards depends on how long immunity lasts and how much the virus changes |
| Latent | The herpesviruses | Shedding without symptoms, disease again at reactivation, and severe disease when immunity is suppressed |
| Chronic | HIV; hepatitis C virus in most infections; hepatitis B virus in most people infected in infancy and fewer infected later (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hbv)); human papillomavirus in a minority of infections | Transmission for years without symptoms, and damage long after infection |

A few of the acute viruses can also persist. Adenoviruses can stay silently in lymphoid tissue, such
as the tonsils, and reactivate to cause severe disease when immunity is suppressed, and hepatitis E
virus can become a chronic infection after an organ transplant.

Persistence has four consequences in medicine:

- A person who carries a persistent virus can transmit it for years, often without knowing of the
  infection, so donated blood and pregnant women are screened for blood-borne viruses.
- Disease can appear years or decades after infection: AIDS after HIV infection; **cirrhosis**
  (scarring of the liver in which bands of fibrous tissue and nodules of regenerating liver cells
  replace its normal structure, so that the liver works poorly) and liver cancer after hepatitis B or
  C virus infection; shingles after chickenpox.
- Every virus on the map that is linked to cancer persists: human papillomavirus, hepatitis B and C
  viruses and Epstein–Barr virus (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cancer)).
- Drugs that block replication cannot remove a viral genome that is not being copied, so they
  suppress some persistent infections without clearing them (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
  targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-few) and, for the hepatitis viruses, [*Blood-borne and
  sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-key)).

The herpesviruses share a genome, an envelope and latency but not a route, whereas the respiratory
and faecal–oral viruses each share a route but not a genome.

## Using the map {#sec-vmap-use}

### The group chapters {#sec-vmap-template}

Each viral group has a chapter of its own, laid out like the bacterial group chapters (see [*A map of
the bacteria*](../bacteria/bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-template)):

| Part of the chapter | Content |
|---|---|
| The group in one sentence | The traits the members share, and the six questions answered for the group |
| Sorting the group | The few traits that separate the members: a tree, a table of what each trait predicts, and a sorting key |
| Main viruses | Two or three viruses, each with its patterns of harm (how a mechanism leads to a kind of damage, with one example), the host, setting and route that let it cause disease, its path through the body on a body map, and a profile card |
| Contrast pair | Two viruses most easily confused, side by side |
| Supporting viruses | One table row each |
| Later in the course | Where the organ-system blocks add diseases, diagnosis and treatment |

Within a group, the members are sorted by the traits that separate them, which are often not the
traits on the map. The herpesviruses, for example, share every trait on the map except route, and
are sorted by the kind of cell in which each becomes latent (see
[*Herpesviruses*](herpesviruses.qmd#sec-herp-key)).

### Reading the map backwards {#sec-vmap-test}

Four of the groups are named for a route, so on this map the route usually points to the group, but
latency outweighs it: varicella-zoster virus spreads in respiratory particles, yet latency places it
with the herpesviruses. Chronic infection points to the blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses.
Given a few traits, name the group.
